worksheet.title: When I Receive
worksheet.subtitle: The message sets the order
worksheet.learning_goal: I can trace which script runs first and which runs when it receives a message.

parts.title: Who goes first?
parts.text: Bit starts on the green flag and ends by broadcasting 'start'. Pixel has the hat 'when I receive start', so Pixel waits until that message comes. That sets the ORDER: Bit runs first, then Pixel runs when it hears the message. Read both scripts and find the order.

parts.title: Which script runs first?
parts.prompt: Which sprite's script runs FIRST — Bit or Pixel? Write it, and write what event starts it.

parts.title: Which runs second?
parts.prompt: Which sprite runs SECOND, and what makes it start? Write the sprite and the event.

parts.title: Where do they land?
parts.prompt: Bit runs from home 1: forward 3. Pixel runs from home 0: forward 2. Where does each land? Bit: ____  Pixel: ____

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A 'when I receive' script does not start until its message arrives. So a broadcast can set the ORDER of two scripts: the sender runs first, and the receiver runs when the message reaches it.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Events & Parallel Scripts
teacher_guide.title: When I Receive
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students trace the ORDER that event-started moves run in. Bit runs on the green flag and sends a message; Pixel waits for that message, so it runs second. The message decides who goes first and who goes next. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer needed — paper and a pencil. You read the prompts aloud. Optional: two counters on a number line 0 to 5 (green Bit, purple Pixel), and a card that says "go" you can hand over to act out sending a message.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Bit runs first (green flag), sends "start"; Pixel waits, so it runs second.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Bit runs first; Exercise 2 — Pixel runs second when it gets the message.
3. Let them try. Students find where each lands (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Bit runs first; its event is "when green flag clicked".
Exercise 2 — Pixel runs second; it starts "when I receive start" (the message Bit sent).
Exercise 3 — Bit: 1, forward 3 → 4. Pixel: 0, forward 2 → 2. Even though there is one green flag, Pixel waits for the message, so the order is Bit then Pixel.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: thinking both start together. Pixel waits for the message, so it is second.
Make it easier: act it out — Bit moves, hands over the "start" card, then Pixel moves.
Make it harder: ask what would make Pixel run first instead.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
In plain terms: students write and run instructions that are started by an event, like clicking the green flag or getting a message.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change what starts them or one move, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child names the run order (Bit then Pixel) and finds both landings.
